Please review the following manuscript. I feel disappointed with this paper. My overall impression is poor, and I'd be concerned to see it accepted.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
out=Path('tmp/pdfs'); out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
pages=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
 t=p.extract_text()
 pages.append(f'\\n\\n======== PAGE {i} ========\\n\\n{t}')
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(pages))
print('PAGES',len(r.pages))
print(''.join(pages[:3]))
PY"

strengths: R2E offers a coherent, useful contribution to biomedical NLP: answer-specific retrieval and a set-based reasoner allow predictions to be attributed to identifiable evidence passages. Training with NULL evidence representations supports the masking operations used for Shapley attribution.

The gene-ranking improvements have support beyond frequency correction. On Gene Description Facts, uncorrected R2E achieves MRR 0.202 versus 0.176 for cosine similarity and 0.167 for MLM; corrected R2E reaches 0.260. Updating the retrieval corpus also improves temporally held-out performance without retraining.

The experimental design includes meaningful safeguards and informative analyses: document-level corpus splits, training from scratch to control pretraining leakage, architectural ablations, and disclosure of weaker results on naturally imbalanced data.

The three released evaluation datasets are valuable resources. The appendices provide substantial detail on objectives, architecture, hyperparameters, prompts, and attribution estimation. These support a Findings-level contribution in inspectable ranking, although broader claims require stronger evidence.
weaknesses: Predictive superiority needs narrower framing. Clinical-trial AUROC is 0.632 for literature-based R2E versus 0.630 for MLM, with no uncertainty reported for that difference. Near-parity is useful for an explainable system, but does not establish a substantial predictive advance. The balanced ranking comparisons also omit a frequency-corrected MLM, despite Appendix G describing that correction. Such a control would better isolate the reasoner's contribution.

Explanation validation is preliminary. Shapley attribution measures dependence on evidence relative to the chosen NULL baseline; it does not establish biological correctness or usefulness to experts. Human validation covers only eight query–target pairs per task, with GPT-4 agreement of 71.5% and 82.2%. Clinical evidence relevance AUROC is only 0.665. Direct human evaluation and comparisons against cosine-based evidence ranking or auditing would strengthen the central explanation claims.

Temporal safeguards are incomplete for the genetics and audited variants. The genetics associations come from a 2023 dataset without a reported restriction to evidence available before the evaluated trials, and GPT-4 auditing may introduce later knowledge. Those results therefore do not establish performance under the historical information constraint used for the literature-only model.

Exact empirical reproduction is substantially constrained. Training data, code, and model weights are withheld, while corpus construction depends on proprietary entity linking and partly licensed literature. Detailed architectural descriptions and public test sets help, but an executable implementation using an accessible corpus would make the central results independently verifiable.

Clinical-development outcomes are an imperfect proxy for target efficacy. Appendix O acknowledges that discontinued programs can reflect commercial or molecule-specific failures, and positive labels include pre-registration. Pooled AUROC across gene–disease pairs also does not directly demonstrate useful target prioritization within a disease. Indication-specific evaluation and sensitivity analyses of outcome definitions would better substantiate the intended application.

Some reporting needs reconciliation. Table S8 gives 0.639 AUROC for the standard corrected literature model, whereas Table 3 reports 0.632 without explaining the difference. Most results lack confidence intervals or variability across runs, and inference and attribution latency are unreported despite their importance when ranking 19,176 candidates.
